newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission adopts communication on copyright.
newsitem.headline: Commission adopts communication on copyright.

text.p: The European Commission promised on Wednesday only limited harmonisation of EU states' copyright law to prevent digital piracy of books, compact discs and videos in the world of computer networks.

Its long-awaited Communication on copyright and related rights in the information society sidestepped demands by the entertainment industry for authors to be given rights to protect the identity and spirit of their work and more money for what is expected to be increased use of the works by broadcasters.

The EU executive, limiting itself to measures which would have a bearing on the single market, said it would propose early next year a directive harmonising rights on the digital copying, communication and distribution of works.

It said it would also propose measures at EU level to prevent people getting round anti-copying systems being developed by industry, although it said it was up to the industries concerned to develop the systems themselves.

Although under existing copyright law it is clearly illegal to copy a tangible video of "Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs", it is less easy to stop people loading and storing the Disney classic on their computer discs once it has been converted into electronic form and transmitted digitally.
The whole works of William Shakespeare along with the Bible and the Kama Sutra can be scanned and copied onto a computer disc and circulated on the Internet.

"In view of the development of new forms of reproduction... there is a need for a clear definition of exactly what is protected as well as an equivalent level of protection across the EU," the Commission said in a statement.

"The Commission will therefore pursue further harmonisation of the reproduction right as a matter of priority. In so doing harmonisation of the limitations/exceptions to the reproduction right will be of the utmost importance."
It said it also wanted to harmonise EU law covering on-demand services in view of their expected growth.

"As the exploitation of works and other protected material in the context of on-demand services will, to a large extent, depend on EU-wide markets and a clear and coherent level of protection...the right applicable to "on-demand" transmissions will have to be harmonised as a matter of priority," it said.
"The Commission will propose protecting digital on-demand transmissions on the basis of a further harmonised right of communication to the public," it said.

It also intends to harmonise rights on distribution, as EU countries have widely varying rules about when an author loses his right, or his right is "exhausted" to veto distribution of copies of his work.
The Commission -- stressing it had limited powers to regulate copyright -- sidestepped other issues of intense interest to the entertainment industry.
"There are a lot of people who think that the Community can replace the national legislation in these cases which is not the case," one Commission official told reporters.
The entertainment industry has been demanding increased remuneration from broadcasting given that in the world of multichannel broadcasting their works will be used more.
The Commission said it did not want to take an initiative until it had held in-depth talks with all parties concerned and that it was not yet clear how multi-channel broadcasting would develop.

A spokesman for the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry said that the question of exclusive rights in multi-channel broadcasting was one of the most crucial questions for the European music industry in the debate on copyright and that the organisation was willing to play its part in the discussion.

The Commission also deferred a decision on whether to harmonise so-called "moral rights", intended to protect entertainers from distortion of the spirit and identity of their works, a practice expected to increase in the information society.

It also said it was too early to rule on whether it was necessary, for example in the case of reproduction of a newspaper on the internet, whether just the newspaper or the individual journalists should be asked for permission.
The Commission said it reached its stance after consulting more than 350 interested parties.
